assessmentSummary.identity: The same ground-start-to-short-acceleration identity, delivered through a 10-metre sprint target.
currentCardFindings: The title adds only a distance dose to the consolidated push-up/prone start.
The description names horizontal push and reorientation but never defines the ground or foot-recovery sequence.
Its generic difficulty values materially understate the upper-body push, reorientation complexity, supervision, and impact.

athleteInstructions: Use the assigned ground-start variant and accelerate through the ten-metre line

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Merge into Push-Up / Prone Start Sprint and retain 10 metres as dosage. Preserve the name as an alias.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Push-Up Start 10m is a acceleration & first-step output exercise for speed, sprinting, and quick-release athletes. It emphasizes horizontal push, hip extension, rapid ground reorientation while keeping the session intent aligned with the Vortex phase sequence.

evidence.sourceTitle: The difference is in the start: impact of timing and start procedure on sprint running performance
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Start procedure and body position influence sprint-start performance and must be specified separately from distance.

Push-Up Start 10m must define chest contact, hand placement, elbow position, cue, lead-foot recovery, push-up or prone transition, sprint distance, and run-out; a cone or 10-metre label does not create a new exercise.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Start push-off and early acceleration are connected but distinguishable portions of a sprint effort.

Push-Up Start 10m belongs to a ground-start-to-short-acceleration family with controlled push-up-bottom and fully prone start-position variants; it is not a conventional push-up set, burpee, reaction test, or cone-agility drill.

evidence.sourceTitle: Sprint Acceleration Mechanics: The Major Role of Hamstrings in Horizontal Force Production
claims: Sprint acceleration requires coordinated hip, knee, and ankle action, including hamstring contribution to horizontal force production.

The ground transition additionally loads pectoral, triceps, shoulder-girdle, wrist, trunk, hip-flexor, and lead-leg recovery functions before gluteal, hamstring, quadriceps, plantar-flexor, foot, and arm-action roles dominate acceleration.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Early acceleration is associated with forward-directed impulse, propulsive force, and progressive projection.

The athlete must clear the hands, recover one foot beneath the body without crowding the knee or twisting, project from the first support, and rise progressively; do not prescribe one universal recovery foot or forced step length.

evidence.sourceTitle: The difference is in the start: impact of timing and start procedure on sprint running performance
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Lower and standing start procedures have different body-position and timing effects.

Exercise difficulty must directly score technical complexity, physical and absolute-load demand, coordination, supervision, failure consequence, impact, work-capacity demand, and overall difficulty; audience experience remains programming context.

evidence.sourceTitle: Correlations between muscle-tendon parameters and acceleration ability in 20 m sprints
claims: Power output is highest during the first sprint-acceleration steps.

Push-Up Start 10m combines upper-body floor push, trunk transition, hip recovery, and high-intent acceleration contacts, so dosage must track attempts, distance, sprint contacts, start-side distribution, wrist and shoulder tolerance, posterior-chain stress, technical fatigue, recovery, and total sprint volume.
Quality sprint work requires a suitable surface, marked target, run-out, spacing, and recovery that preserves speed quality.

Require a clean non-abrasive hand-contact surface, clear dry sprint lane, safe separation, appropriate footwear, target, and run-out; wrist, elbow, shoulder, trunk, and acceleration readiness must match the chosen ground-start variant.
Acceleration sessions should prescribe distance, intensity, repetitions, sets, and recovery rather than repetitions alone.

Use 2-5 high-quality starts over 5-15 metres with roughly 90-180 seconds recovery, alternating intended recovery side when appropriate; use slower transition rehearsals separately from maximal sprint attempts.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Start setup should support effective projection without forcing an anthropometrically inappropriate position.
Use a small cue set: set hands and chest exactly, push the floor away, recover one foot beneath the hips, clear the hands, project forward, coordinate the arms, and sprint through the target.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Training should use qualified supervision, correct technique, manageable demands, and gradual progression.

Stop for wrist, elbow, shoulder, chest, back, hip, hamstring, knee, ankle, or foot pain; head or knee contact; hand slip; failed foot recovery; stumble; lane obstruction; marked speed loss; collision risk; or unsafe run-out.
Acceleration and maximal velocity are distinct qualities, and start work should not become dense conditioning.

Push-Up Start 10m belongs after joint and sprint preparation and before fatiguing work; use a slower ground-transition drill for learning and high-intent full starts only when the athlete can recover cleanly and accelerate safely.
Acceleration develops across successive steps rather than by immediately standing upright.

Show side and front views of exact hand, chest, and elbow setup, both lead-foot recoveries, the transition at slow and full speed, first three contacts, finish, run-out, and a two-point-start regression.
Coaches should distinguish acceleration output from maximal-velocity and conditioning work.

Provide setup checks, side and front observation, start-side distribution, transition time if measured, first-step and distance counts, lane and floor inspection, upper-limb symptom gates, speed-loss stops, and exact duplicate or variant decisions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Speed work should be developmentally appropriate and based on movement competency.

Accessibility options include a two-point start, elevated hands, hands-and-knees transition rehearsal, slower cue, chosen lead foot, shorter distance, submaximal intent, untimed attempts, extra demonstration, and longer recovery.

evidence.sourceTitle: The difference is in the start: impact of timing and start procedure on sprint running performance
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Start position and timing procedure can change the task and measured result.

Ten metres, five-to-ten yards, and a cone target are dosage or logistics; chest fully supported versus bottom push-up position, elevated hands, external cue, partner contact, and added push-up repetitions require controlled variants or distinct definitions.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.

Candidates for Push-Up Start 10m remain unapproved. Current embedding, exact prone or push-up-bottom setup, complete viewing, captions, instructional quality, safety, reviewer identity, and approval remain separate gates; unrelated cone and build-up videos are excluded from the replacement packet.
